title: Epidemiology of DSM-5 alcohol use disorder: Results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions III

claims.statement: In adults aged 18 or older living in US households and some group homes, a national face-to-face survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 36,309 people, 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared) found DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, diagnosed with a structured interview given by lay interviewers, in 13.9 in 100 adults in the past year (SE 0.31) and in 29.1 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild (7.3 in 100 adults mild, 3.2 moderate, 3.4 severe). The disorder was more common in men than in women (17.6 against 10.4 in 100 in the past year) and at ages 18 to 29 (26.7 in 100) than at 65 or older (2.3 in 100). Among adults who had drunk alcohol in the past year, 17.5 in 100 (95% CI 16.7 to 18.3) met the older DSM-IV criteria in the same survey, as did 54.5 in 100 of those who had drunk heavily at least once a week (4 or more US standard drinks of 14 g of alcohol in a day for women, 5 or more for men) (Grant et al., 2017). The figures depend on the survey: another national survey, cited by the same authors, found 7.0 in 100 adults with the disorder in the past year in 2013, about half the NESARC-III figure, and the authors do not explain the difference. NESARC-III left out homeless people, people in prison and most people in treatment, which the authors say may lower its figures, and 4 in 10 of the people sampled did not take part. By the older DSM-IV definition, the same institute's surveys found 8.5 in 100 adults with the disorder in 2001–2002 and 12.7 in 100 in 2012–2013, but the two surveys differed in design and response (81.0% against about 60%) and the other national survey showed a stable figure of about 7.5 in 100 over 2002 to 2013, so these studies cannot show whether the disorder became more common. For the world, a narrative review relays WHO estimates for 2016 of 5.1 in 100 people aged 15 or older (8.6 in 100 men, 1.7 in 100 women), which its authors call rough estimates; these figures are second-hand (Carvalho et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Grant et al. 2015 (NESARC-III, weighted, % (SE)): past-year DSM-5 AUD 13.9 (0.31): mild 7.3 (0.19), moderate 3.2 (0.13), severe 3.4 (0.12); lifetime 29.1 (0.48): mild 8.6, moderate 6.6, severe 13.9; past year men 17.6, women 10.4; ages 18–29 26.7, 30–44 16.2, 45–64 10.0, 65 or older 2.3; lifetime men 36.0, women 22.7. Response 60.1% (screener 72.0%, person 84.0%). National Survey on Drug Use and Health, as cited: past-year AUD 7.0% in 2013, about 7.5% and stable over 2002–2013. Grant et al. 2017 (DSM-IV, past year, % (95% CI)): 2001–2002 8.5 (8.0–8.9), 2012–2013 12.7 (12.1–13.3), a difference of 4.2 percentage points (editors' calculation; the paper gives only the relative change, 49.4%); among people who drank in the past year 12.9 (interval printed as 12.3–17.5, a misprint) and 17.5 (16.7–18.3); among people who drank heavily at least weekly 46.5 (44.3–48.7) and 54.5 (52.7–56.4); response 81.0% (2001–2002) and 60.0% (2012–2013; 60.1% elsewhere in the paper). Carvalho et al. 2019, relaying WHO: 2016, ages 15 or older, men 8.6% (8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); high-income countries 8.4% (8.0–8.9), upper-middle-income 5.4% (5.0–6.0).

claims.statement: In US adults with DSM-5 alcohol use disorder in a national household survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared), 7.7 in 100 of those who had the disorder in the past year and 19.8 in 100 of those who had had it at some time said they had sought treatment or help for it, counting 12-step groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (the abstract calls this being treated). Seeking help rose with severity: 4.4, 8.7 and 34.7 in 100 of people with mild, moderate and severe lifetime disorder. Among people with the disorder in the past year, 4.5 in 100 had used 12-step groups, 3.6 in 100 a health care practitioner, 2.0 in 100 an outpatient service and 1.8 in 100 a rehabilitation programme. For other countries, a narrative review relays, second-hand, that 22.3 in 100 patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries received interventions, and 21.9 in 100 worldwide in an overview published in 2004 (Carvalho et al., 2019; two authors declare fees or grants from companies, including drug companies, outside the work). Help-seeking was self-reported at one interview, the survey did not cover most people who were in treatment, which would lower its figures, and 4 in 10 sampled people did not take part. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Grant et al. 2015 (NESARC-III): sought treatment or help, 7.7% (12-month DSM-5 AUD) and 19.8% (lifetime); DSM-IV 8.1% and 15.6% (2001–2002 NESARC: 7.2% and 14.0%); by severity, 12-month 2.7%, 4.9%, 21.3% and lifetime 4.4%, 8.7%, 34.7% (mild, moderate, severe); sources among 12-month AUD: 12-step groups 4.5%, health care practitioners 3.6%, outpatient facilities 2.0%, rehabilitation programmes 1.8%; lifetime AUD: rehabilitation 9.0%, practitioners 8.7%; mean age at first treatment 29.4 years. Carvalho et al. 2019 (second-hand): 22.3% of patients identified with alcohol dependence in primary care in six European countries received interventions (more than 13 000 patients, 358 general practitioners); 21.9% in a global overview (2004).
